raw_response:
I would start by evaluating Zulip, especially because keyboard access matters to you. Mattermost and Rocket.Chat are additional direct team-chat candidates. If ordinary channel chat is sufficient, The Lounge paired with an open-source IRC server offers a different architecture.

1. **Zulip** — https://zulip.com/features/

   Zulip has an open-source server and clients, supports self-hosting, and supplies a web interface plus iOS and Android apps. Its official feature matrix explicitly lists extensive keyboard shortcuts. Conversations are organized into topics inside channels, which can help keep parallel discussions separate but requires a different habit from a flat Slack channel. The official Zulip 2.1 announcement dated December 13, 2019 confirms an open-source server, an installation route and mobile/desktop apps before your question date: https://blog.zulip.com/2019/12/13/zulip-2-1-released/. The current shortcut and feature matrix should not be treated as a complete snapshot of the 2020 version.

2. **Mattermost, using its open-source edition** — https://github.com/mattermost/mattermost

   The official repository documents self-hosted deployment, a web interface, and Android/iOS clients. It is a strong candidate for a conventional team-chat setup. Choose the appropriate open-source edition and check the feature boundaries for the version you deploy: commercial enterprise editions also exist. I did not verify that most features can be operated without a mouse. The official 5.23 announcement is dated May 18, 2020, so the product was available before the question date: https://mattermost.com/blog/mattermost-5-23-automatic-hyperlinking-to-jira-issues-and-more/. Current client documentation is separate evidence and does not establish historical availability of every feature.

3. **Rocket.Chat, using the community/core configuration** — https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat

   Its official README describes deployment on your own servers and access through web and mobile apps. The core repository uses the MIT license, with explicit exceptions for enterprise directories and third-party components: https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/blob/develop/LICENSE. Limit an all-open-source installation to the appropriate core components. Native mobile source licensing and broad keyboard operation were not separately audited here. The evidence opened is live and undated; I have not established the exact feature set available on June 24, 2020.

4. **The Lounge plus InspIRCd** — https://thelounge.chat/ and https://www.inspircd.org/

   The Lounge is a self-hosted, MIT-licensed web IRC client whose interface supports desktops, smartphones and tablets. Pair it with the GPLv2 InspIRCd server to control both sides of the system. The Lounge stays connected while a browser is offline, allowing users to resume their sessions. This is useful if your essential need is channel-based messaging, but it requires two components and an evaluation of IRC's differences from Slack. I did not verify broad keyboard coverage or a dated pre-2020 feature snapshot.

My first trial would be Zulip because it provides the clearest documented match for your optional keyboard requirement. For the others, the required browser/mobile and self-hosting arrangement is documented, while the edition boundaries and unverified points above deserve checking before choosing one.
limitations: Searches and live sources were retrieved in November 2026 for a question dated 2020-06-24. Dated historical sources establish Zulip and Mattermost product availability, not every current feature.
Rocket.Chat and The Lounge/InspIRCd evidence remains date_status=unknown; a live page was not backdated merely because the project is old.
Unauthenticated grep.app access was attempted and blocked. Indexed GitHub materials were retrieved using code-through-web fallback; native code search did not succeed.
The optional requirement that most features work without a mouse was not exhaustively tested; Zulip's documented extensive shortcuts are the strongest verified match.
